overview: Both are the liquid part of blood, but serum is what's left after clotting removes the clotting factors.
genZNote: Plasma: blood's full liquid portion, clotting factors included. Serum: same liquid, minus the clotting squad that already did its job.

aspects.label: Clotting Factors Present?
aspects.valueA: Yes — plasma retains fibrinogen and other clotting factors.
aspects.valueB: No — serum is plasma after clotting has removed fibrinogen and clotting factors.

aspects.label: How It's Obtained
aspects.valueA: Obtained by centrifuging blood treated with an anticoagulant.
aspects.valueB: Obtained by letting blood clot naturally, then centrifuging to separate the liquid from the clot.

aspects.label: Relative Volume
aspects.valueA: Slightly larger volume, since clotting factors are still present.
aspects.valueB: Slightly smaller volume than plasma from the same blood sample.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: Serum is used for many diagnostic blood tests specifically because it lacks clotting factors that could interfere with certain assays.
overlay.memoryTrick: Serum has already 'served its clotting duty' — the clotting factors are gone.
overlay.commonMisconception: Serum is not the same as whole blood minus cells — it's plasma minus clotting factors, so it still contains most other plasma proteins.
